title: The Small Things That Survived: Sarajevo's War Childhood Museum
listening_note: A 12-minute guide to a museum where a toy, a pair of shoes, or a razor can tell a fuller story of war than a monument can.
story_html:
Begin with the size of the thing in front of you

Before you begin reading the labels, look at the scale of the objects around you. A shoe. A photograph. A letter. A toy that might once have fit in one hand. The War Childhood Museum does something deceptively simple: it asks you to meet war through the possessions that children, or former children, held onto. Not through a map of front lines first. Not through a list of military units. Through the stubborn physical life of ordinary things.

That choice changes the tempo of the visit. A museum of war can make a visitor feel that history is a wall of information: vast, terrible, already finished. Here, the object interrupts that distance. A small item is never only evidence. It is also a relation. Someone kept it, carried it, repaired it, or chose to give it away decades later. The question to hold as you move through the rooms is not simply, what happened here? It is: what did a child need in order to keep a sense of a life beyond what was happening?

This is not a museum that makes childhood innocent in a decorative way. The stories can involve siege, displacement, bereavement, and genocide. But its central insight is more precise: children were not just symbols of suffering. They were people improvising routines, loyalties, play, taste, fear, and hope under conditions they did not choose.

A city under siege, seen at child height

The Sarajevo exhibition grew out of the Bosnian war of the 1990s, when children across Bosnia and Herzegovina lived through radically different forms of danger: the siege of Sarajevo, forced displacement, refugee life, separation from family, and the violence of the Srebrenica genocide. The museum does not pretend that these experiences were identical. Its Bosnian collection draws from more than thirty towns, not only Sarajevo. That matters. The city around you is the museum's home, but the stories refuse to turn one city's experience into the whole history of the war.

You may already have visited the Tunnel of Hope or looked down across Sarajevo from a fortress. Those sites explain how a besieged city was cut off and how people moved through it. This museum changes the camera angle. It asks what that condition did to a school day, a sibling relationship, a birthday, a habit of making music, or the meaning of a pair of shoes.

It is useful to notice what you will not find at the centre of the room: a single official voice telling you what the war means. The museum is built from first-person testimony. Its method is deliberate. A contributor's object is paired with the story that gives it meaning. The institution describes its work as documenting and digitising lived experience, while its researchers are trained to work with sensitive testimony. That does not make memory simple or complete. It does make the authority of the exhibit different. Instead of asking you to admire a curator's conclusion, it asks you to listen to a person explain why this thing mattered.

From one question to a museum

The museum began with a question asked by Jasminko Halilović, himself a child during the war. In 2010, he invited people who had grown up in wartime Bosnia to answer a short prompt about what war childhood had meant to them. The responses became the book War Childhood: Sarajevo 1992-1995. As the project developed, people did not only send memories. Many still had objects: diaries, letters, photographs, clothing, toys, improvised household items. The book opened a door; the objects showed how much memory was still living in kitchens, drawers, and family cupboards.

That origin matters because it explains the museum's tone. It was not built by collecting examples of childhood from a distance. It was built through former children deciding what they could bear to name and what they wanted preserved. The permanent exhibition opened in Sarajevo in January 2017. Since then, the institution has grown beyond Bosnia and Herzegovina, documenting childhoods affected by conflict elsewhere as well. But Sarajevo remains the place where the idea becomes most immediate: a museum made inside a post-war city by people whose childhood memories were once treated as private, peripheral, or too small for history.

The project also has a tension worth noticing. Personal testimony is not a shortcut to consensus. Bosnia and Herzegovina still carries competing political narratives about the war. A recent independent report describes the museum as working in an environment saturated by nationalist rhetoric. Its response has not been to flatten difference into a comforting slogan. It has been to preserve a multiplicity of lived accounts, and to make room for dialogue through particular lives rather than abstractions.

What an object can hold

Now slow down at one display. Do not try to absorb every story at the same emotional volume. Pick one object and let it take its time. Ask three questions: what was this thing before the war, what did it become during the war, and what does it mean now that it has entered a museum?

A story from the collection follows a pair of ballet shoes. Their owner, Mela, remembered wanting the usual pink pointe shoes and receiving white ones made in Sarajevo before the war. Her teacher explained that they were part of a local theatrical world that the war had interrupted. The shoes do not need to become a grand metaphor to matter. They hold the very ordinary disappointment of a child who wanted to fit in, then the discovery that her own pair belonged to a city with a cultural life and a future that war could damage but not erase. The object makes room for jealousy, ambition, instruction, and attachment. In other words, it gives childhood back its complexity.

Another collection story centres on a father's razor carried out of Srebrenica by a family after he was killed in the genocide. It is a hard object to look at because it joins an everyday act, shaving before work, to an irreversible absence. The museum does not ask you to turn away from that fact. But it also does not let the person disappear into a number. The razor remains connected to a father remembered as neat and clean-shaven, to a family who saved it, and to a son who eventually chose safekeeping over private possession.

And then there are objects that describe survival without turning it into triumph. A suitcase packed by a girl told she was going to the seaside became part of a forced journey out of a city. A blue toy rabbit brought joy in a refugee camp after a child lost her brother. A young musician remembered forming a band during the war because music gave friends a way to be together. These are not interchangeable tales of resilience. They are records of people making narrow spaces of agency inside circumstances that had taken away so much control.

Why the museum rotates its stories

The exhibition changes each year. That is not only a practical decision about a growing collection. It is an argument against the idea that war childhood can be represented by one definitive set of objects. The museum's permanent exhibition selects personal stories around different facets of experience, and its wider collection holds thousands of objects. An annual rotation lets a visitor encounter aspects that a previous selection could not contain: shelter, play, loss, clothing, danger, migration, friendship, or the strange work of trying to resume a routine.

That approach is also a useful check on the visitor. You are not being asked to leave with a single emotional verdict. Sadness is appropriate here, but sadness alone can become passive. The more demanding question is what it means to hear someone else's account without using it up as an illustration of a lesson you already had. Read the name. Notice the date of birth if it is given. Notice where a story stays specific rather than explaining everything. Let the contributor's language set the scale.

The museum has been recognised internationally, including with the Council of Europe Museum Prize in 2018. That recognition is meaningful, but it is not the reason the place works. The force of the museum is smaller and more difficult: it trusts that a visitor can sit with an object and a first-person account without being rushed into spectacle. It gives personal memory a durable public form while acknowledging that no collection can contain the whole of war.

Carry one question back into Sarajevo

When you leave, the streets outside may look ordinary again: people carrying bags, waiting for a tram, speaking with friends, moving toward dinner. That ordinary life is not a distraction from the museum. It is part of what the stories make newly visible. Childhood during war was not an existence outside ordinary life. It was ordinary life forced into impossible conditions.

Before you go, return to one object you almost passed too quickly. Look once more at its material: worn fabric, plastic, metal, paper, a trace of use. Then ask what changed when its owner decided that it should no longer remain only in a private drawer. The museum's answer is not that an object can repair the past. It cannot. Its quieter claim is that attention can resist erasure. In a city where history is often visible on a grand scale, this is a place that asks you to remember at human scale.
